key-west: Key West is about four hours' drive from Miami on the Overseas Highway, so it is not an easy day trip. The island has few natural sandy beaches; people come for the water, the boats and Old Town, not a long beach. Late October brings Fantasy Fest, ten days of adult costume parades that take over Duval Street and push room prices to their peak, so check the calendar before booking.
miami-beach: Miami Beach is its own city across the bay from Miami, and South Beach is only one part of it. In March, spring break crowds bring curfews, checkpoints and heavy policing to South Beach in some years, and in early December Art Basel fills every hotel. Quieter stretches like Mid-Beach and North Beach have the same ocean with far fewer people.
orlando: Orlando is more than the theme parks, but if the parks are why you are coming, timing matters more than anything. School holidays, spring break and the weeks around Christmas bring the longest lines and highest prices, and summer means near-daily afternoon thunderstorms that close outdoor rides. With Epic Universe now open alongside Universal and Disney, plan which parks you want before you book a hotel, because the resort areas are far apart.
tampa: Tampa is a city on the bay, not a beach town; the Gulf beaches of Clearwater and St. Pete are 30 to 45 minutes away and the bridges back up on weekends. The Riverwalk downtown is the easiest way to see the city on foot. In late January, Gasparilla's pirate parade closes Bayshore Boulevard and draws hundreds of thousands of people, so plan around it or plan for it.
st-augustine: St. Augustine is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the US, and its historic core is small, walkable and short on parking. From late November through January, Nights of Lights brings heavy traffic and long waits downtown, especially on weekends. Park once and walk, or use a remote lot and the trolley.
fort-myers: Fort Myers and Fort Myers Beach are different places about 30 minutes apart, and the beach town is still rebuilding after Hurricane Ian in 2022. Some hotels, restaurants and landmarks there are new, rebuilt or still under construction, so check that what you are booking is open. Winter, when seasonal residents arrive, brings the heaviest traffic on the roads to the islands.
sarasota: Sarasota's beaches are on the barrier keys, not in the city itself, and Siesta Key is still recovering from the 2024 hurricanes, so some businesses and beach facilities have changed. Season runs roughly January through April, when traffic to the keys is heavy and rooms cost the most. Summer is quieter and cheaper but brings heat, afternoon storms and red tide risk in some years.
naples: Naples is a quiet, upscale Gulf town, and its beach access is mostly through small public lots and street parking that fill early in season. Winter brings seasonal residents and the busiest restaurants and roads, from about January through Easter. Sunsets from the pier and the beach ends of the downtown streets are the main event, so plan to be there by early evening.
daytona-beach: Daytona Beach lets you drive on parts of the beach, but only in marked zones, during set hours and for a daily fee, and tides can close those zones. Bike Week in March and Biketoberfest in October bring hundreds of thousands of motorcycles, noise and booked-out hotels. Race weeks at the Speedway, especially the Daytona 500 in February, do the same.
new-orleans: New Orleans is much more than Bourbon Street, which most locals avoid. Mardi Gras is a weeks-long season of parades across the city, not a single day, and hotels fill and parade routes close streets for much of it. Hurricane season peaks from August through early October, and summer heat and humidity are intense, so many visitors prefer late fall and spring.
nashville: Nashville's Lower Broadway is built for visitors, with bachelorette parties and party wagons most weekends; many locals spend their nights in East Nashville, the Gulch or 12 South instead. In early June, CMA Fest fills downtown hotels and pushes prices to their highest of the year. The Grand Ole Opry is in Music Valley, about 20 minutes from downtown, not on Broadway.
austin: Austin's big events reshape the whole city: SXSW in March and Austin City Limits over two October weekends fill hotels and raise prices sharply. Summer days often top 100°F, so locals swim at Barton Springs or hit the lakes rather than walk around at midday. Sixth Street is mostly bars for visitors; many locals head to Rainey Street, East Austin or South Congress.
san-diego: San Diego's beaches are often overcast in late spring and early summer, a pattern locals call May Gray and June Gloom, so the sunniest beach weather is usually late summer and fall. Comic-Con in July fills downtown hotels and pushes prices up sharply for that week. Neighborhoods are spread out, so pick a base by what you want: the beaches, downtown, or La Jolla.
charleston: Charleston's historic peninsula floods at very high tides and in heavy rain, and some downtown streets close when it does. Spring, especially during the Spoleto Festival in late May and June, is the busiest and most expensive time to visit. Summer is hot and humid with frequent afternoon storms, and hurricane season runs through fall.
savannah: Savannah's Historic District is best seen on foot through its squares, but downtown parking is limited and enforced. St. Patrick's Day is one of the largest celebrations in the country here, and hotels fill and prices jump for that week. Summer is hot and humid, and gnats are a well-known nuisance from spring into summer.
las-vegas: Las Vegas resort fees and parking charges can add a lot to the advertised room rate, so compare the total price before you book. Big conventions and the Formula 1 Grand Prix in November push room prices up and bring road closures on and around the Strip. Summer days regularly pass 110°F, so plan outdoor trips to Red Rock or the Hoover Dam for early morning or the cooler months.
new-york: New York is five boroughs, and many of the places locals love are outside Midtown. Driving into Manhattan below 60th Street now carries a congestion toll, so the subway is usually the faster and cheaper choice, and you can tap a card or phone to pay. Times Square is best seen once and left; the weeks between Thanksgiving and New Year's bring the biggest crowds and highest hotel prices.
chicago: Chicago's lakefront beaches are only staffed with lifeguards in summer, roughly Memorial Day through Labor Day, and swimming outside that window is not allowed. Winter is long and cold, with wind off the lake making it feel colder than the thermometer says. Summer festivals like Lollapalooza fill hotels, so book early for July and August.
san-francisco: San Francisco summers are often cool and foggy, especially near the ocean and the Golden Gate, so pack layers even in July. September and October are usually the warmest, clearest months. Neighborhoods change block by block and the hills are steep, so plan walking routes and use transit for the long climbs.
seattle: Seattle's rainy reputation comes mostly from October through April, when days are gray and drizzly rather than stormy; July through September are usually dry and mild. Pike Place Market is busiest on summer weekends and when cruise ships are in, so go early. Many of the region's best views and hikes are an hour or more away, so leave time to get out of the city.
denver: Denver sits at about 5,280 feet, so altitude, sun and dehydration hit visitors harder than they expect. Rocky Mountain National Park, about two hours away, uses a timed-entry reservation system from late spring to mid-fall, so book that before you go. Spring snowstorms are common through April and even May.
honolulu: Honolulu is a real city on Oahu, and Waikiki is only one small part of it. Popular spots like Diamond Head and Hanauma Bay require advance reservations for visitors, and they sell out. Trade winds keep most days pleasant year-round, but winter brings big surf to the North Shore and the holidays bring the highest prices.
asheville: Asheville and the surrounding mountains are still recovering from Hurricane Helene in 2024, so check that trails, roads and businesses are open before you go. Some sections of the Blue Ridge Parkway near Asheville have reopened and others remain closed for repairs. October leaf season is the busiest and most expensive time to visit.
